newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong investors turns nose up at mutual funds.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong investors turns nose up at mutual funds.

text.p: Hong Kong people, who enjoy a reputation worlwide for canny investment, are shunning mutual funds and stolidly ignoring the retirement savings craze sweeping the United States and Europe.
Mutual fund managers in Hong Kong are scratching their heads trying to figure out ways to make their products more appealing.

"You can get everything here that you can get in other markets but we just haven't had the savings into unit trusts that they've had in other economies," said Christopher Ryan, managing director of HSBC Asset Management.

Less than four percent of Hong Kong residents invest in mutual funds or unit trusts, even though surveys by the Hong Kong Investment Funds Association show that most people are aware that these funds exist.
By comparison, in the United States, 30 percent of the population invests in mutual funds.

Most fund managers in Hong Kong said the domestic funds industry is suffering from a lack of incentive. In the United States and Europe, awareness that public pension schemes are underfunded prompted a wave of regulatory change to encourage individuals to provide for their own retirement.

"A lot of the growth in the mutual fund market in the U.S. in the last few years is as a result of the popularity of the tax benefit associated with 401Ks (savings incentive), so it's not necessarily a level playing field," said Ryan.
"Here, in a sense, we are competing on a level playing field with all other forms of investment. In other countries, they're not."
Hong Kong, with its low tax rates and lack of savings incentives, offers plenty of investing alternatives.

"One is the stock market which is cheap, understandable and easy to use. The other one is Happy Valley (race course), which is easy to use, understandable and cheap. Unit trusts have none of these features. We're working on it, though," said Christopher Day, joint managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd.
Fun is an important factor for Hong Kong investors, said Gary Greenberg, deputy managing director of Peregrine Asset Management.
"Just as it's more fun to pick a horse, it's more fun to pick a stock, especially when everything continually goes up," Greenberg said.
Hong Kong's stock market has offered steady returns over the past two years, with the Hang Seng index rising to new record highs recently.
Hong Kong fund managers have adopted different tactics to counter the lack of enthusiasm at home.
Peregrine said it is focusing instead on larger markets in the United States and Europe, while Thornton is working hard to make its products more accessible.
Day said assets for the top 12 companies in the United States grew by 41.8 percent in 1995 to about US$460 billion.
"That kind of savings power is not something one just ignores," he said.
